summary: The note describes salt block grilling, an ancient technique using heated Himalayan salt slabs as a cooking surface, and its modern revival among chefs and home cooks. Drawing on September 2023 encounters in Charleston, South Carolina, it covers heating, searing, flavor, chilled uses, care, and the communal, theatrical appeal. It also notes a growing community, workshops, and rising sales of salt blocks.
one_line: Salt block grilling, an ancient Himalayan-salt cooking method, is enjoying a modern revival, with tips on heating, flavor, chilled dishes, safety and care.
key_facts: Salt block grilling uses a large piece of pink salt, typically sourced from the Himalayas, as a cooking surface that imparts subtle saltiness.
Chefs like Francis Mallmann and food writer Mark Bitterman introduced the technique to a broader audience.
The author visited James and Deirdre McCarthy in Charleston, South Carolina, by September 18th, 2023, to learn the fundamentals.
James McCarthy, a retired chef, says to heat the block slowly, starting with a low flame and gradually growing to high heat, to prevent cracking from thermal shock.
A well-heated salt block can sear, sauté, and even serve cold dishes, according to James McCarthy.
Elena Torres, a local chef who began using salt block techniques in late 2023, says salt blocks reach higher surface temperatures than most grilling surfaces, producing an iconic sear.
Scallops cooked on the McCarthys' hot block developed a golden-brown crust with tender interiors.
Deirdre McCarthy served thin watermelon slices, fruits and cheeses on a chilled salt block.
Pastry chef Myles Becker gave a dessert demonstration on September 25th, serving strawberries and cream on a chilled salt block.
Craft markets and kitchen stores are seeing a notable uptick in sales of salt blocks, and Elena Torres leads culinary workshops on cooking with them.
The McCarthys stress handling blocks with heat-resistant gloves and allowing plenty of time for them to cool after use.
Myles Becker advises wiping a used block with a moist cloth and gently scrubbing residue, avoiding drowning it in water because it can dissolve.
